question.knowledge_point: Determining Whether a Vector Lies on a Plane
question.problem: Determine if the vector $u$ lies on the plane $Π:r=sb+tc,$ $t,s\in R$, where  $b=⟨1,-1,3⟩$, $c=⟨-2,4,-3⟩$, and  $u=⟨3,-7,3⟩.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of $s\cdot t$ from the decomposition $u=sb+tc.$
question.worked_solution:
By definition, $u\in Π$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}sb+tc & =u \\ s[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4 \\ -3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -7 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s-2t=3 \\ -s+4t=-7 \\ 3s-3t=3\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ -1 & 4 & -7 \\ 3 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 \\ 3 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & 3 & -6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & -6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s-2t=3 \\ t=-2 \\ 0=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
t=-2.
$$

Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s-2t & =3 \\ s-2(-2) & =3 \\ s+4 & =3 \\ s & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we found a solution $s=-1,\,t=-2,$ we conclude that $u$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have

$$
u=-b-2c.
$$

Finally, $s\cdot t=(-1)\cdot (-2)=2.$

judgment.reasoning: Every selected answer agrees with its own captured final solution. No grading evidence is supplied. Two source defects remain: q-105261 labels a row scaling as -1/2 although its displayed result requires +1/2; q-127043 has two mathematically correct radio choices, options 1 and 2, because opposite nonzero vectors are both parallel to the line. Its worked solution explicitly supports option 1. Independently, q-34218 has the unique decomposition b=2a1+4a2-2a3, giving product -16. In q-74558, every vector in the span has equal first and third coordinates, requiring k=0; coefficients (2,1) establish sufficiency. In q-74560, every vector in the span has third coordinate twice its first, requiring k=-24; coefficients (-2,-2) establish sufficiency. In q-105248, the first and third equations force s=1,t=-1, but these give second coordinate 6 rather than 5, so u is outside the plane. In q-105261, u=-b-2c gives st=2. The selected vectors in q-34142 and q-105291 are respectively -3a1 and a1/3. In q-34276, a3=a1-a2 proves dependence, so only III is true. In q-105315, determinant -6 proves independence, so II and III are true. Separating constants and coefficients of t gives the vector equations in q-36023 and q-127002. The coefficients of t give parallel vectors in q-32785 and q-127043. For q-32817, the image shows P=(-1,3,2) and Q=(2,4,5); Q-P=(3,1,3), giving the selected parametric equations. Earlier answers for recurring questions remain valid; q-32817 now uses the current escaped-brace choice value. None of the final source answers is mathematically wrong.
